records.name: Gambia
records.summary: Gambia is dangerous for trans visitors. There is no LGR and no visible community.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Gambia has criminalised same-sex conduct since the colonial era; the 2014 amendment introduced 'aggravated homosexuality' (life imprisonment) under Jammeh, who threatened to 'decapitate' gay people. A new criminal code (March 2025) removes 'aggravated homosexuality' but sets a minimum of five years for 'unnatural offences' (defined as 'any homosexual act') and three years for 'gross indecency', with no maximum - so any same-sex act could in theory draw life. The Barrow government has not typically enforced.
West Africa Democracy Radio: 'Gambia increases minimum sentence for homosexual acts to 5 Years' — reports the new criminal-law package raising the minimum sentence for same-sex acts to five years.

Freedom House Freedom in the World 2024 for The Gambia: 'Partly Free' (50/100); freedoms improved under Barrow after 22 years of Jammeh's rule, but LGBT+ people face severe discrimination among ongoing concerns.

UK Home Office CPIN Gambia: Sexual orientation and gender identity or expression (v3.0, Feb 2023): assessment of risk, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with detailed country information on law and treatment.
HRW report (Sept 2015) 'State of Fear': arbitrary arrests, torture and killings in Gambia under Jammeh - includes the context of his anti-gay rhetoric and threats against LGBT people.

US State Department 2020 Human Rights Report for Gambia: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised (up to life imprisonment under the 2013 amendment); documents arrests and societal discrimination.
US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Gambia: official assessment - continued criminalisation, no prosecutions reported, significant societal stigma and police harassment of LGBT persons.

freshness.fact: Still criminalised (S.158, up to 14 years; women added 2005; 2014 'aggravated homosexuality' carries life; no legal gender change)

records.name: Guinea-Bissau
records.summary: Guinea-Bissau demands real caution. Same-sex conduct is legal (one of few West African states never to criminalise); no LGR, no protections; chronic instability (coups) and weak state; documented social hostility but no mob-lynching pattern of Benin's type.

sources.claim: US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Guinea-Bissau: documents the 2012 coup, arbitrary killings, torture, drug-trafficking-linked corruption and impunity - general context; no criminalisation of same-sex conduct.
US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Guinea-Bissau: documents security-force torture, FGM, impunity - general context; the LGBT section notes no criminalisation but societal stigma.

Everything Explained summary of LGBT rights in Guinea-Bissau: legal since 1993 (new penal code decree 4/93 omits same-sex offences); signed the 2008 UN SOGI statement; only heterosexual married couples entitled to larger government housing; domestic-violence law (6/2014) Article 5 protects victims regardless of sexual orientation.
LiquiSearch: LGBT rights in Guinea-Bissau - brief overview page (Wikipedia-derived) noting legal challenges and sections on same-sex activity, relationships, adoption and living conditions.

Mapa.gay country guide for Guinea-Bissau: legal since 1993; no partnership recognition; limited protection via domestic-violence law; no trans framework; travel-safety score 34/100 ('Caution'); 9% consider homosexual behaviour morally acceptable - unusually moderate for West Africa; no visible LGBT scene; some violence cases reported (2018).

freshness.fact: Legal since 1993, no relationship recognition or protections — current overview still says exactly that; cited 2009-2017 reports' legal baseline unchanged (social-stigma framing remains apt).

records.name: Equatorial Guinea
records.summary: Equatorial Guinea is dangerous for trans visitors. The 2022 penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex conduct — but a 2024 Synergía report documents twelve women imprisoned between January and August 2024 in police raids led by the Armed Forces and State Security, with detention-for-bribes and indefinite imprisonment; a Draft Law “Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals” (2020, status unclear) would formally criminalise. Africa's longest-ruling dictatorship; no recourse.

sources.claim: Synergia report on lesbophobia, human rights and police raids in Equatorial Guinea: documents police and military interventions in spaces of assembly, expression and residence of lesbian women; in Bata, police detain known lesbians collectively ('lesbians are members of a sect'), including collective punishment when one lesbian is sought.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): the 2022 penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy or gender diversity, but a Draft Law Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals (2020, status unclear) would effectively criminalise LGBTIQ people; authorities still apply the obsolete 1954 Law on Vagrants and Criminals, which normalises conversion practices and classifies homosexuality as illness; three legal instruments institutionalise discrimination (Military Justice Code, ministerial order on 'immoral' activities, provincial regulation).

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Equatorial Guinea: official assessment - same-sex conduct not specifically criminalised but LGBT persons face societal stigma; no anti-discrimination protections; general repression context.
Canada IRB Response to Information Request on Equatorial Guinea: country-of-origin research citing publicly available information on conditions relevant to refugee claims.

UPR stakeholder submission (Small Media, EG Justice, IPI, Digital Rights in Equatorial Guinea) for Equatorial Guinea's fourth review: focuses on freedom of expression, digital rights and journalist safety - the repressive environment that also constrains LGBT advocacy.

Hispanic Studies Review (Oct 2025): academic article on Equatoguinean queer motherhood in Trifonia Melibea Obono's novel 'Yo no quería ser madre' (2019) - compulsory heterosexuality and queer invisibility in Equatorial Guinea.

freshness.fact: 2022 Penal Code made same-sex sexual activity LEGAL and added Equatorial Guinea's first explicit sexual-orientation employment protections; legal gender change still not recognised

records.name: Greece
records.summary:
Greece is a workable destination with a clear law-versus-practice gap. The legal framework is among Europe's strongest — it ranks 7th on the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map, has banned conversion therapy and intersex infant surgery, has a hate-crime law covering gender identity, and legalised same-sex marriage in 2024 (the first Orthodox-majority country to do so). There are no trans-specific border or bathroom restrictions, and the government is progressive with an improving trajectory.

But the social reality lags the law. A mob of about 150 people assaulted two trans people in Thessaloniki; an European Court of Human Rights case documented police detention and mistreatment of trans sex workers; surveys show Greeks are markedly more avoidant of public LGBTI visibility than the EU average (63% avoid holding hands); and the UK Foreign Office has issued an LGBTQ travel warning for Greece.

Major tourist destinations — Mykonos, Athens's Gazi district, Thessaloniki — are welcoming; outside them the climate is rougher than the law suggests.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Greece: the marriage-equality law (5089/2024) added SOGIESC equal-treatment guarantees in goods/services, education, healthcare and housing; in March a mob of ~150 attacked two trans people in Thessaloniki (21 arrested, 11 minors), followed by a masked attack on counter-protesters; the Orthodox Church officially opposed marriage equality; transphobic comments targeted Eurovision contestants; 'Family Pride' counter-demonstrations were organised.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Greece: the ECtHR condemned Greece for the treatment of an LGBTI Iranian refugee detained pending deportation (Article 3 violation); a criminal case was opened over an online post inciting discrimination against immigrants and LGBTI people; in July the Crete Court of Appeal convicted three French tourists for a 2017 attack.

ILGA-Europe case-law page on Koutra and Katzaki v. Greece (ECtHR app. 459/16, 2017): detention and mistreatment of transgender sex workers and their lawyer by Greek police in 2013 - police stops of trans people on the street and removal from cars; complaints against officers were discontinued; third-party intervention by ILGA-Europe, TGEU, Greek Transgender Support Association and ICRSE.

PinkNews (April 2024): the UK Foreign Office updated its Greece travel advice for LGBTQ+ holidaymakers - same-sex relations legal, civil unions since 2015, marriage since February 2024 (first Orthodox-majority country), age of consent 15 for all, and transgender people able to change legal gender; travellers advised to remain alert.

EU FRA LGBTIQ survey III country sheet for Greece (2024): 63% avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (EU-27: 53%); 36% avoid certain locations for fear of assault (EU-27: 29%); 35% are open about being LGBTIQ (EU-27: 51%); 28% felt discriminated at work (EU-27: 19%).

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Greece ranked 7th in Europe on the 2025 Rainbow Map; conversion practices banned for minors and IGM criminalised (2022); National Strategy for LGBTQI+ Equality; 2023 anti-bullying education law and employment-discrimination ban on SOGI; February 2024 Law 5089/2024 extended equal-treatment grounds (SOGIESC) across social protection, education, healthcare, housing and goods/services, alongside marriage equality.

The Press Project (May 2025): TGEU's Trans Rights Index & Map 2025 shows backsliding outpacing progress across Europe for the first time; Greece meets 21 of 32 indicators - gaps include age restrictions on name changes, no national action plan, and no legal recognition of trans/non-binary parenthood.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex marriage legal since 2024; adoption and foster care; discrimination and hate-speech protections; gender identity and expression (self-ID since 2017); conversion therapy; military service; correctional facilities; social conditions including Pride events and homophobic violence.

PinkNews (April 2008): Greece's Justice Ministry pledged a working group on the rights of cohabiting gay couples, to 'analyse all aspects of the issue, international practice and the existing domestic legal and social framework'; the government said it would include same-sex unions in upcoming unmarried-couples legislation.

freshness.fact: Marriage equality upheld by Supreme Court May 2025 (ruling published March 2026); self-ID gender recognition since 2010, depathologised 2017; NEW Apr 2025 surrogacy ban for gay/single men

records.name: Grenada
records.summary: Grenada demands real caution. The buggery law (10 years) remains on the books (no successful court challenge yet), though unenforced; no LGR; small community; tourist areas insulated.

sources.claim: NOTE: This HRW article is about Antigua and Barbuda's 2022 ruling, not Grenada specifically; included as Eastern Caribbean regional context.

The Advocates for Human Rights + Khaleem Ali + GrenCHAP UPR stakeholder report (Oct 2024) on LGBTIQ+ rights in Grenada: GrenCHAP has served marginalised groups (LGBT+, PLHIV, sex workers, vulnerable youth) for over 15 years; documents the legal and social situation for the UN review.

Outright International country overview for Grenada (updated March 2026): same-sex conduct criminalised under Sections 430 ('grossly indecent act') and 431 ('unnatural crime'); no legal gender recognition; no anti-discrimination protections; LGBTIQ people face discrimination in housing, education, employment and public services, harassment and violence; fear of prosecution inhibits reporting to police.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Grenada: significant human-rights issues include laws criminalising consensual sexual conduct between men, though not enforced; otherwise no arbitrary killings, torture or disappearances reported.

records.name: Greenland
records.summary:
A self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts for domestic law. Its LGBT record is quiet and consensual: partnership law came from the Danish model in 1996 with virtually no debate; marriage equality was adopted from Danish legislation in 2016, passed unanimously by the local parliament with the established church's bishop supportive; and in 2016 the territory took a self-declaration approach to gender recognition, ahead of the metropole's own practice.

For a visitor the picture is low-friction: gay life is described as 'almost a non-event' — integrated, non-violent, modest, with a small Pride since 2010 and a national equality association (Qaamaneq, 2014). The counterweight is capacity, not hostility: some 56,000 people across remote settlements means thin institutional reach, and anonymity comes from isolation rather than crowds.

sources.claim: Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Sept 2024) on Denmark's decade of self-ID - included for Greenland as part of the Danish Realm; Greenland adopted its own gender-recognition framework based on self-declaration in 2016.

Outright International country overview for Denmark (updated March 2026), included for Greenland as part of the Danish Realm: robust protections, self-determined gender markers, SOGISC discrimination protections.

GlobalGayz 'Gay Greenland - Past and Present' (May 2015): gay life in Greenland is 'almost a non-event' - low-key, integrated, non-violent; modest Pride march since 2010; the 1996 same-sex partnership law passed with virtually no debate - a picture of quiet tolerance.

PinkNews (April 2016): Greenland's same-sex marriage law came into effect - adopted Danish legislation, passed unanimously twice (first bill lapsed due to Danish elections); replaces the 1996 Danish-derived partnership law; Bishop Sofie Petersen supported it.

KNR Greenlandic Broadcasting (Aug 2014, in Danish): new national association LGBT Qaamaneq founded for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people - aims for political, cultural and social equality; open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters.

records.name: Guatemala
records.summary:
Guatemala demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: Asociación Lambda's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022, with 35 victims saying they intended to flee the country. Guatemalan officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds they are not “biological women.” There is no legal gender recognition and no SOGI hate-crime statute (a 2022 law actually increased penalties for “aggravated” LGBT visibility before being struck down).

Congress has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives (Law 5276, the 2022 “Life and Family Protection” law, later shelved after protests). The community is organised (Lambda, trans collectives) but under pressure. Tourist areas (Antigua, Atitlán) are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from the general violence level.

sources.claim: Wikipedia article on transfemicide (killing of trans women motivated by transphobic/misogynistic hatred): regional coverage includes North and South America; relevant background for Guatemala's context of violence against trans women.

Arcus Foundation report (May 2024): the Inter-American Court's 2017 gender-identity opinion (Advisory Opinion OC-24/17) advanced legal gender recognition in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, but a growing, vociferous opposition movement seeking to define gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash in all four countries.

HRW (Jan 2022): 'Guatemala: Anti-Trans Bill Threatens Rights' - documents legislative attacks on trans people, including bills that would erase gender identity protections and restrict legal recognition.

Washington Blade (Jan 2018): Latin American countries, including Guatemala, urged to abide by the landmark Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruling (Advisory Opinion OC-24/17) requiring marriage equality and gender recognition.

records.name: French Guiana
records.summary:
Full French framework applies as an overseas department: same-sex marriage (2013), anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, simplified administrative gender-marker change since 2017, and hate-crime sentence provisions — nothing criminalises being trans, and Pride is held in the main city with a small but visible community.

The friction a trans visitor meets is practical rather than legal. Specialised gender-affirming healthcare is thin and remoteness pushes residents into metropolitan France for care; local reporting describes conservative community norms and cultural taboos that discourage visibility and reporting. The sharpest documented state machinery is custodial: the national watchdog on places of detention found persistent, serious violations against transgender prisoners, and investigative reporting details how trans women incarcerated by legal-gender assignment fall through procedural cracks — practice that applies in the territory as in the hexagon. A current-status review adds locally elevated violent crime against a backdrop of a visible, tourism-oriented economy: ordinary-visitor caution is warranted, trans-specific state action is not documented.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018, French context): trans women in France incarcerated on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal gray area - relevant to French Guiana as a French overseas region applying French law.

CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty (French context, applicable in French Guiana): serious violations persist across places of detention.

Grokipedia page on transgender rights in French Guiana: France's national framework applies - simplified legal gender recognition since 2017 (administrative declaration, no surgery/sterilisation/diagnosis required), anti-discrimination protections since 2012, hate-crime provisions 2017; but specialised trans healthcare is limited by remoteness; societal transphobia and cultural taboos discourage visibility and reporting.
Gayther country guide for French Guiana - LGBTQIA+ travel and country information (page largely navigation/index content).

GayOut travel guide for French Guiana: same-sex relations legal, same-sex marriage legal (French law), Pride events held; rated 'Very Safe for LGBTQ+'; no listed venues - a small scene anchored in Cayenne.
Gayther LGBTQIA+ country guide for French Guiana - equality index, gender-identity recognition, same-sex unions and marriage data (page largely navigation/index content).

freshness.fact: Full French framework applies: decriminalised 1791, marriage 2013, no-surgery self-declaration gender recognition (2017); locally higher violent crime, visible tourism economy
